Abstract Various proxy data agree on a shallow Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) during the last glacial maximum (LGM), extending down to 2000 m − 2500 m depth, which is similar to the AMOC geometry projected by climate models over the 21 st century with rising atmospheric CO 2 .
The AMOC strength in the two climate states is insufficiently constrained.

Introduction The AMOC is part of the global Meridional Overturning Circulation (MOC), which is a major component of the climate system.
Introduction The AMOC is part of the global Meridional Overturning Circulation (MOC), which is a major component of the climate system.

In a zonally averaged view, the MOC can be divided according to the region of deep-water formation into the North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) cell characterised by northward flow in the upper ocean and southward flow in the deep ocean 1 , and the Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) cell with northward flowing water in the abyssal ocean below the NADW cell.

In a zonally averaged view, the MOC can be divided according to the region of deep-water formation into the North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) cell characterised by northward flow in the upper ocean and southward flow in the deep ocean 1 , and the Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) cell with northward flowing water in the abyssal ocean below the NADW cell.
The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM, ~21,000 years before present) is one of the best documented periods by paleoclimate archives and helpful for understanding past climate change and carbon cycle 7 .

During the LGM, the AMOC was shallower relative to the present-day AMOC by about 1000–1500 m, which is a robust feature inferred from various types of tracers such as δ 13 C, Cd/Ca, PO 4 and εNd 8 – 13 .

57 report that CMIP6 models that form dense water via shelf processes and with parameterised overflows around the Antarctic are the most accurate in capturing the properties of the present-day AABW.

Our findings reinforce that improving the representations of shelf processes and density-driven overflow in climate models is crucial to understand past and future changes in the deep waters and hence the AMOC geometry.

Since reconstructions and modelling studies 67 – 70 of the glacial AMOC strength are subject to large uncertainties, we constrain the changes in the AMOC strength using the present-day overturning pathways.

Our approach is primarily based on the hypothesis that climate models fully capture the dynamical processes underlying the response of the overturning pathways to external forcing across climate states.

It is worth noting that the relative contributions of the two pathways to the AMOC changes vary across climate states, which result from differences in the westerly winds and Southern Ocean stratification.
The glacial AMOC strength is hence subject to large uncertainties.

Relative to the CMIP5 models, the larger correlations of the AMOC changes with the Indo-Pacific pathway in the CMIP6 models is possibly due to improvements in the parameterisations of mixing processes and mesoscale eddies 38 , 76 , and/or from increased model resolution 77 , 78 .
Of particular importance to understand the spread of the glacial AMOC strength across models may be the parameters affecting vertical mixing.

The version of the KCM used here consists of the ECHAM5 83 atmosphere general circulation model with a horizontal resolution of T42 (2.8° × 2.8°), and with 19 vertical levels reaching up to 10 hPa.
